questions.question: Criticize the effectiveness of tables in Power Point / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Tables are not very effective when used in PowerPoint, except when they are very small.
  • The size of the cells and the space available reduce readability. It is visually far more

questions.question: Differentiate role of eye contact and posture in active listening . / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Eye contact
  • Just as a speaker should provide selective eye contact to the listeners, the listener should
  • provide periodic and selective eye contact to the speaker. The same benefits of eye contact
  • that apply to a speaker also apply to a listener.
  • Posture
  • The best posture for effective listening is to sit bending a little forward. This shows a sense of
  • anticipation.
  • If there is a table in front of you, leaning forward with your elbow every now and then will be a
  • good posture for listening.
  • Make sure you don’t get physically tired of whatever posture you choose. Else, your focus will
  • only be on your physical discomfort and not on the subject matter you are listening to.

questions.question: Briefly Illustrate the effect of emphasis and how emphasizing different words can result in presenting different messages / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Emphasis of words is another important tool. When you have a sentence, not every word in
  • the sentence is equally important. By emphasizing certain words, you can get the correct
  • meaning across. If you utter all the words with the same stress, it becomes monotonous and
  • each audience member could potentially walk away with totally different interpretations of
  • your message. By emphasizing different parts of a sentence, very different meanings can be
  • conveyed.

questions.question: Explain the importance of postures in a conference / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Posture refers to how you stand or sit. This is a sure give-away of your attitude and
  • confidence level. When you are standing straight and not slouching, it usually indicates a
  • higher degree of confidence. When shoulders droop or when you are bending forward too
  • much, it conveys a lack of confidence.
  • Posture also applies when you sit. Leaning forward while sitting down could indicate a more
  • keen interest in the subject matter. When you extend the leaning forward to almost lying
  • down on the table, it will obviously convey a reduced interest in the subject.
  • Whether you are sitting or standing, a good posture would:
  • Be comfortable for you
  • Demonstrate your active interest and confidence
  • Not hinder other communication vehicles (like gestures, movements, etc.)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Distinguish between the types of synchronous communication / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Synchronous communication can again be classified into face-to-face communication and
  • non-face-to-face communication. The meetings you attend, the interviews you conduct,
  • the presentations you make and the classes you conduct in the classroom are all examples
  • of face-to-face, synchronous communication.
  • In the second category of synchronous communications comes non-face-to-face
  • synchronous communication. These are the telephone calls and the chat sessions
  • that you have. Here, you face all the challenges that you come across in the face-to-face
  • case, with one more added challenge: you have lost those valuable cues of body
  • language. You don’t have any mechanism to fathom the implied meaning of any spoken
  • word For example, you cannot look at the enthusiasm (or lack thereof) in the gestures and
  • body language. You would not be able to look into the eyes of the recipient to make a
  • judgement as to whether or not he is lying.

questions.question: What is interpersonal communication? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• First, for communication to qualify as interpersonal, at least two people must be
  • involved.
  • Second, interpersonal communication is a process. By this, we simply mean that it
  • usually involves a series of actions: Kelli talks/Jason listens, Jason responds/Kelli
  • listens, and so on.
  • Third, this process is interactional. Effective communication is not a one-way street:
  • Both participants send as well as receive information when they’re interacting.
  • Communicators also interpret and create messages by reflecting on their own
  • experiences.

questions.question: List the objectives of effective communication. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Communication establishes an ongoing relationship between two parties—the sender and
  • the receiver: In most cases, communication is never a one-time deal.
  • There may be a series of interviews you would have to go through to get a job; you would
  • almost never close a deal in one shot with a customer.
  • True communication is seldom a one-off transactional thing.
  • Every communication is made up of a series of communication cycles: Each of these
  • cycles contributes to the objective, and builds upon the previous cycle.
  • Each communication cycle is a brick carefully laid with other bricks to achieve the
  • objective of communication.

questions.question: Describe the components of vocal variety. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• There are certain important constituents of a good voice channel. These are:
  • • Pronunciation and Articulation - Pronunciation refers to your ability to utter the words
  • in the same way as is considered standard..
  • • Articulation refers to coherence of the words and phrases in a talk. When a person
  • is articulate, the message would be easier to understand for the audience. Articulation
  • stems from proper pronunciation but is more than mere pronunciation.
  • • Emphasis –When you are speaking, not everyone in the audience tunes in to your
  • speech the way you think they should.
  • • Pace – Pace refers to how fast you speak.
  • In general, in many cases, higher the pace of speech, the more persuasive it is.
  • Higher pace gives an aura of confidence for the speaker but also gives less opportunity
  • for the audience to intervene.
  • • Pitch- Pitch refers to how shrill your voice is – the baseline frequency of your
  • voice.
  • The pitch of your voice is dictated by the thickness and length of your vocal chords.
  • Each of our voices has some limits within which we can ‘stretch’ them.
  • Too much of stretching will be physically painful for the speaker and may be jarring for
  • the listener.
  • • V olume –Volume refers to the loudness with which you speak.
  • Some people habitually speak so loud that you wish you had a remote control button for
  • controlling their volume!
  • At the other extreme are people who talk so softly that they can barely be heard even
  • when you sit close to them. To be effective you need to strike a balance.
  • Volume goes in tandem with other parameters like speed, pitch, and articulation.
  • • Pause- A good presentation should not be a continuous outpouring of words
  • without any gaps.
  • Periodic pauses during a presentation are essential. These enable you to recover your
  • breath and also enable the audience to reflect on what you have said.

questions.question: Explain the concept of assertiveness and discuss why assertiveness training is important, especially for women. / [CO5] [2x7=14]
questions.solution_html:
• Concept of Assertiveness
  • • Many people have a hard time being assertive; however, this problem is more common
  • among females because they are socialized to be more submissive than males—to “be
  • nice.” Generally, people tend to associate assertiveness with direct person-to-person
  • social interactions.
  • • Assertiveness is also important in indirect exchanges as well. Learning to be assertive in
  • email or text messages or on social networking sites is also important.
  • • Assertiveness involves acting in one’s own best interests by expressing one’s thoughts
  • and feelings directly and honestly.
  • • Essentially, assertiveness involves standing up for your rights when someone else is
  • about to infringe on them.
  • • Submissive communication is deferential, as it involves giving in to others on points of
  • possible contention. Submissive people often let others take advantage of them.
  • • Typically, their biggest problem is that they cannot say no to unreasonable requests.
  • • A common example is the college student who can’t tell her roommate not to borrow her
  • clothes.
  • • Submissive people also have difficulty voicing disagreement with others and making
  • requests themselves. In traditional trait terminology, they are timid.
  • • They appear to lie in excessive concern about gaining the social approval of others.
  • • Aggressive communication focuses on saying and getting what one wants at the
  • expense of others’ feelings and rights. With assertive behavior, however, one strives to
  • respect others’ rights and defend one’s own.
  • • The problem in real life is that assertive and aggressive behaviors may overlap.
  • Assertiveness training is especially popular among women. Men, too, find assertiveness
  • training helpful, both because some have been socialized to be passive and because others
  • want to learn to be less aggressive and more assertive.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
